Generally, the word simply means "recent" or "new": what exists for a short time and has not had time to age or wear out.
G4372.origine: The word comes from a Greek root that carries the idea of what is "fresh" or "recent." The original image is that of something alive, that has just occurred. In Hebrews 10:20, Paul uses it to convey the idea from Psalm 81 and Deuteronomy: what is new in the biblical sense is often what comes from God, what has not been worn out by sin or old practice.
G4372.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament according to the Segond 1910: in Hebrews 10:20, where Paul speaks of the "new and living way" that Christ has inaugurated for us through the veil — that is, by passing through his own body. The context shows that "new" does not simply mean "recently appeared," but rather "fresh," "living," "unworn": it is a way that did not exist before, which gives access to the very heart of God. This new path contrasts with the old ways of the Old Covenant and their ritualism.
G4372.portee: For the Christian, this word invites us to discover the radical newness of access to God through Christ. It is not our works that open the way for us: it is a path that Jesus alone has inaugurated, a living and inexhaustible way. It also speaks to our experience: each day, this path remains fresh, always effective, never aged by time or habit.

sens: At a time not far from the present, not long ago
Of recent date, for a short time
G4373.detail:
1. This word indicates that an event occurred not long ago, in the near past. In Acts 18:2, Aquila and Priscilla had just left Rome after Emperor Claudius had expelled the Jews from the city — it was a recent departure, of which Paul learned the circumstances in Corinth.
2. The adverb emphasizes the new or fresh character of a situation. The couple was still in the very early stages of their life in Corinth, freshly arrived from Italy: this explains why Paul met them and worked with them, as if he were seeing distressed refugees.
G4373.origine: The adverb comes from the Greek adjective *prosphatos* (fresh, new). This family of words evokes the idea of what has just happened or been born — a sense that recalls the Hebrew *hadash* (new), which is found in the Greek Old Testament (Deuteronomy 24:5 speaks of a "new" wife). The basic image is that of novelty, of what has not had time to age.
G4373.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 18:2. Paul arrives in Corinth and meets Aquila and Priscilla, a couple of Jews who had just arrived from Italy fleeing Claudius's expulsion decree. The historical context gives the word its full weight: Aquila and Priscilla were not established residents, but recently displaced refugees, which makes their meeting with Paul all the more significant — they shared the same trade (tentmaking) and became companions of the missionary.
G4373.portee: This word reminds us that God often acts through impromptu meetings, born of recent and painful circumstances. The flight of Aquila and Priscilla was a distress — an imposed exile — but it placed them on the road to Paul at the exact moment he needed it. For the reader, it is a lesson in humility: the "recent" events of our lives, even difficult ones, can be the prelude to providential encounters that bring us closer to God and his people.

sens: To bring someone or something before a person, to present it
To present an offering, a gift, or a sacrifice to God
To make a sacred oblation, a cultic act in honor of God
To offer one's life, to give oneself as a sacrifice
G4374.detail:
1. The primary meaning is concrete: to physically bring a person or thing to someone else, to present it to them. Jesus heals the sick whom people "bring" to him (Matthew 9:32), or children whom they "present" to him (Mark 10:13). Joseph and Mary offer a bird at the temple to fulfill the law (Luke 5:14). 
2. In a religious context, "to offer" means to present a gift, a prayer, or a sacrifice to God. The Magi "offer" gold, frankincense, and myrrh to the child Jesus (Matthew 2:11). A believer must "offer" their gift to God before presenting it at the altar (Matthew 5:23). 
3. The word designates the sacramental act of offering at the temple: a sacrifice, an oblation, prayers. The high priest "offers" sacrifices for his sins and those of the people (Hebrews 5:1, 3). This act is at the heart of ancient worship. 
4. For Christ, "to offer" expresses the supreme gift: he "offered himself once for all" to bear the sins of all (Hebrews 9:28). Abraham "offers" his son Isaac, a picture of the willing sacrifice (Hebrews 11:17).
G4374.origine: The Greek word combines the prefix "pros-" (toward, before) and the root "pher" (to carry, to bring). Its image is that of carrying something toward a person, handing it to them. In the Septuagint, it primarily translates the Hebrew "qarab" (to approach, to offer), a key verb in Israelite worship. The noun "prosophora" (offering) derives from it, as does the simple verb "phero" (to carry). This root evokes the action of presenting or presenting oneself to God with a gift, a prayer, or oneself.
G4374.emploi: The word appears 45 times in the New Testament, mostly in the Gospels and the Epistle to the Hebrews. In the first three Gospels, it means "to bring": sick people are brought to Jesus for healing (Matthew 4:24, 8:16, 9:32). In Matthew and Mark, it can mean "to present" in the sense of putting forward (Matthew 22:19). In the Epistle to the Hebrews, the cultic meaning predominates: the high priest "offers" sacrifices (5:1, 9:7), Jesus "offers" himself once for all as a perfect sacrifice (9:28, 10:12). In John 16:2, "to offer worship" means to give honor. The word emphasizes the presentation before God or before a person of authority.
G4374.portee: This word reveals the vertical relationship with God: one "offers" what is most precious (gold, frankincense, myrrh, prayer, life) before him. For the Christian, it reshapes worship: Jesus has "offered" the unique and perfect sacrifice that renders all other sacrifices obsolete. Learning this word means understanding that true worship consists of presenting oneself and what one possesses before the Lord with a sincere heart.

sens: That inspires affection, kindness
That pleases, that is enjoyable to be around
What deserves to be loved
G4375.detail:
1. The word describes a person or thing that naturally provokes affection and sympathy in those who know it. It is something that attracts love or kindness.
2. More broadly, it refers to what is pleasant, enjoyable to live with or to associate with — not necessarily of striking beauty, but of a quality that makes relationships easy and sweet. In Philippians 4:8, Paul invites Christians to focus their thoughts on everything that is "lovely": he speaks of what truly deserves to be loved and considered, what nourishes a life of goodness.
3. The word also carries the idea of what earns approval, what is worthy of esteem precisely because it inspires affection rather than mere respect or fear.
G4375.origine: The word comes from "philéô," which means "to love, to cherish." The prefix "pros" indicates a direction, a tendency: literally, "toward love." It is therefore a word that speaks of what naturally turns toward affection, or what affection turns toward. It is a rare word in the New Testament.
G4375.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament, in Philippians 4:8. Paul lists the qualities on which Christians should focus their thoughts: whatever is true, honorable, just, pure, and lovely. In this list, "lovely" occupies a special place: it designates what pleases, what inspires affection, in contrast to what might be merely respectable or imposing. It is an invitation to cultivate thoughts that nourish goodness and love, not just moral rigor.
G4375.portee: For the Christian, this word reminds us that moral life is not reduced to duty or rectitude: it also embraces what is beautiful, what inspires gentleness and love. By cultivating thoughts on what is lovely, one nourishes a heart capable of tenderness and kindness toward others. It is an invitation to an attractive virtue, not just an austere one.

sens: The act of presenting, offering something to God
A gift, a present offered to God or to a superior
A sacrifice or material gift presented at the temple according to the Law
Figuratively: what one gives of oneself as a gift to God
Believers offered to God as a living offering
G4376.detail:
1. Offering primarily refers to the act of presenting, bringing something to God as a sign of respect, gratitude, or repentance. It is the gesture of approaching God with a gift (Acts 21:26 speaks of "the offering presented for each one").

2. The word also designates the gift itself, the material present brought. In the time of the Law, it was often an animal (sacrifice) or produce from the land (Hebrews 10:5, 8 lists "sacrifices, offerings, burnt offerings").

3. In the Jewish temple worship, the offering was regulated by the Law: Paul goes to the temple to perform the offering rites related to a vow (Acts 24:17).

4. Jesus himself "gave himself...as an offering" to God (Ephesians 5:2): his sacrifice replaces all former sacrifices, as he willingly offers himself.

5. Believers also become an offering: "that the Gentiles might be an acceptable offering to him" (Romans 15:16) means that God receives converts as a precious and sanctified gift.
G4376.origine: The Greek word προσφορά comes from προσφέρω ("to bring toward, to offer"), composed of πρός ("toward") and φέρω ("to carry"). It literally means "a bringing toward God." In biblical Hebrew, this word often translates מִנְחָה (minha, "offering, gift"), which generally refers to a non-blood gift, and sometimes פָּנִים (panim, "face") in the expression "bread of the face" offered before God at the temple.
G4376.emploi: The word appears 9 times in the New Testament, mainly in the epistles and Acts. In Acts, Paul speaks of concrete offerings at the temple (21:26, 24:17): this is the classic use in Jewish worship. In the epistles, the meaning broadens and becomes theological: in Romans 15:16, the offering is spiritual (the converts themselves), while in Ephesians 5:2, it is Christ's sacrifice that is described as an offering. The Epistle to the Hebrews (10:5, 8, 10, 14, 18) systematically contrasts the old offerings of the Law with Christ's unique and definitive offering, showing that his sacrifice has rendered all other sacrifices unnecessary.
G4376.portee: This word helps the believer understand the heart of Christ's sacrifice. Jesus did not offer himself reluctantly or out of obligation, but willingly, "as a fragrant offering" pleasing to God. It also teaches us that we ourselves are called to be an "acceptable offering" to God, that is, to give ourselves entirely to him — not through rituals, but through a living consecration of our hearts and actions.

sens: Speaking to someone, addressing them with words
Calling someone, summoning them by name
Addressing a group to gain their attention or engage in conversation
G4377.detail:
1. The primary meaning is to direct one's speech toward someone, to speak to them directly. Jesus "addresses" a sick woman to help her (Luke 13:12), Pilate "speaks" to the crowds to propose something (Luke 23:20), and Paul "speaks" to the multitude from the steps of the fortress (Acts 21:40). It is a directed, intentional exchange.

2. Sometimes the word means to call or summon someone by name to come. Jesus "calls" his disciples and chooses twelve to be his apostles (Luke 6:13): he expressly designates them.

3. In other contexts, it involves addressing a group to attract their attention or to engage in dialogue. Children "speak" to one another in the public square (Luke 7:32, Matthew 11:16) — it is mutual and direct communication.
G4377.origine: The word is composed of the prefix "pros-" (toward) and "phonéô" (to make a sound, to cry, to speak). The basic image is that of the voice going toward someone. This construction suggests a directed and voluntary communication. The Greek word is used to translate particularly Hebrew or Aramaic forms expressing the action of speaking to someone in a deliberate and direct manner.
G4377.emploi: The verb appears 7 times in the Gospels and Acts. In Matthew 11:16 and Luke 7:32, children "speak" to one another. Luke 6:13 describes Jesus "calling" his disciples — an act of designation. In Luke 13:12 and 23:20, it is Jesus and Pilate who "address" their interlocutors. Acts 21:40 and 22:2 show Paul "speaking" to a crowd. The word can govern a dative (listening person) or an accusative (person or group addressed), which does not change the meaning: always the idea of a word directed toward someone with intention and in their presence.
G4377.portee: This word reminds us of the importance of addressed speech in the New Testament. Jesus "addresses" the sick, the disciples, those who suffer — not from a distance, but face to face, with a precise intention. It is a word of encounter and dignity: the one who is addressed is not ignored, they are recognized and targeted. For a Christian, it invites a responsible and directed speech, never vague or detached.

sens: Action of pouring or spreading a liquid over something
Religious rite of sprinkling blood or water
Application of a liquid substance in fine droplets
G4378.detail: 1. Concretely, a sprinkling is the action of pouring or projecting liquid onto a surface or a person — one sprinkles, spreads drop by drop or in a spray. 2. In the Israelite religious context, sprinkling specifically refers to the rite of pouring blood on altars or sacred objects. At Passover, Moses commanded the Israelites to sprinkle the blood of the lamb on the lintel and doorposts (Hebrews 11:28): it is the sprinkling of blood that marked the houses of believers and preserved the firstborns from the plague. 3. More broadly, the gesture signifies consecration and protection — marking something or someone by sprinkling means setting it apart for God and placing it under His care.
G4378.origine: The word comes from the Greek πρός (toward) and χύσις (the action of pouring, spreading), which is based on the verb χέω (to pour). It is therefore literally a "pouring toward" or "pouring over." This vocabulary of pouring characterizes the rituals of purification and consecration in the worship of the God of Israel.
G4378.emploi: The word appears only once in Hebrews 11:28, in a passage that enumerates the acts of faith of the ancient believers. Paul celebrates the faith of Moses who, by performing the sprinkling of blood at Passover, believed in God's word and His promise of protection for the firstborns of Israel. This passage connects the ancient rite to the very heart of faith: obeying God through actions that signify total trust in His power and mercy.
G4378.portee: For the Christian reader, the sprinkling of blood at Passover foreshadows the protection and purification that the blood of Christ brings to the believer. The ritual gesture also invites understanding that true faith is not measured by feelings, but by concrete obedience to God's words, even when one does not yet see how they will be fulfilled.

sens: To make physical contact with something with a fingertip or part of the body
G4379.detail: 1. To touch means here to establish a light physical contact, with a fingertip. Jesus reproaches the teachers of the law for loading men with heavy burdens to bear, but they themselves do not even "touch" them with a finger (Luke 11:46). The image is one of such minimal contact that a single finger would suffice, to show hypocrisy: they demand from others without sacrificing anything themselves.
G4379.origine: The Greek word prospsauō is formed from the prefix pros (toward) and psauō (to touch). It appears mainly in poets and later writers. The simple verb psauō evokes a light contact, like a caress or a brushing. This composition reinforces the idea of a direct and immediate contact.
G4379.emploi: This verb appears only once in the New Testament, in Luke 11:46. Jesus uses it to describe the attitude of the teachers of the law toward the religious obligations they impose: they do not want to "touch" these burdens, meaning neither to bear them nor to lighten them, even with a symbolic gesture. The word emphasizes their complete refusal to participate in the sacrifices they demand from others.
G4379.portee: This passage invites the believer to examine their integrity: do we demand from others what we are not willing to live or bear ourselves? To touch the burden means to acknowledge its reality and to partake in the common load. It is a call to authenticity and solidarity in obedience.

sens: Treating someone preferentially or unfavorably based on their appearance, wealth, or social status rather than according to justice
Showing partiality in favor of the powerful or against the weak
G4380.detail:
1. The word evokes the image of a judge who looks at the face (the prestige, wealth, social position) of the one appearing before him, instead of judging according to the law. It is to show favoritism or partiality: treating someone better because they are rich, influential, or of high rank, and treating another worse because they are poor or insignificant. In James 2:9, showing favoritism is clearly presented as a sin, a violation of God's law which demands equality and justice for all.

2. By extension, it refers to any form of discrimination or unequal treatment based not on merit or truth, but on external criteria: appearance, wealth, reputation, social rank. One who acts this way shows that they respect the world and its values more than God and His justice.
G4380.origine: The word is composed of two elements: "prosōpon" (the face, appearance, the person) and "lambanō" (to take, to receive). The basic image is "to receive the face" or "to accept according to the face" — that is, to judge based on appearances. This expression translates the Hebrew "nasa panîm," literally "to lift the face" before someone, which means in the Old Testament to show undue favor or partiality (see Leviticus 19:15).
G4380.emploi: This verb appears only once in the New Testament, in James 2:9. The apostle James uses it to forbid believers from showing partiality in favor of the rich at the expense of the poor in the Christian assembly. It is at the heart of James' teaching on the impartiality required by authentic faith: if you prefer the powerful or the wealthy, you violate the royal law of loving your neighbor and become transgressors. The context shows that this favoritism is incompatible with faith in Jesus Christ and brotherly love.
G4380.portee: This word reminds the believer that God does not show favoritism and calls His disciples to imitate Him: to treat each person with dignity and justice, regardless of their wealth, power, or appearance. It is an invitation to purify one's heart of all favoritism and discrimination, and to live the brotherly equality that the Gospel proclaims.

sens: The act of considering someone based on their appearance or social status rather than on justice
Bias in favor of a person, favoritism
Unjust judgment based on superficial human criteria
G4381.detail: 1. The word literally refers to the act of 'taking into consideration the face' or the outward appearance of someone. It is treating someone differently based on their social status, wealth, prestige, or condition rather than on truth and justice. In Acts 10:34, Peter acknowledges that 'God shows no favoritism': this means that God does not judge according to human criteria of power or prestige. 2. The term more broadly describes an unjust bias in favor of certain people. It is showing favoritism or partiality based on who you are rather than what you do or what is right. 3. It is an unequal judgment or treatment based on appearances or superficial criteria: one looks at the 'face' (position, appearance) and not the heart or justice.
G4381.origine: The Greek word is composed of two parts: 'prosōpon' (face, appearance) and 'lēptēs' (one who takes). The basic image is therefore that of 'one who takes into consideration the face.' The root 'to take the face' expresses the idea of treating someone differently based on their outward appearance or social position. It is a concept forged to express the contrast between God's justice, which does not look at appearances, and human weakness that succumbs to it.
G4381.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament: in Acts 10:34. Peter pronounces it after his vision of the sheet filled with unclean animals and the visit of the messengers from the centurion Cornelius. In this decisive context, Peter recognizes that his own Jewish culture had led him to a 'respect of persons': he considered the Gentiles to be unclean and unworthy. But God showed him that this distinction was unjust. The phrase 'God shows no favoritism' becomes a fundamental principle: God welcomes all people according to their hearts, not according to their origin or status.
G4381.portee: Peter's words remind the reader that any favoritism or judgment based on appearance goes against the nature of God. It frees the Christian from human respect and concern for appearances, turning them toward justice and the equal dignity of all before God. It invites treating each person according to truth, not according to their position or prestige.

sens: Advantage or preferential treatment given to someone based on their appearance, status, or wealth rather than on justice
Attitude that judges or favors certain individuals based on unjust external criteria
Lack of impartiality before God or the law
G4382.detail: 1. It is the act of treating someone differently — better or worse — because they are rich, powerful, beautiful, from a good family, or for other reasons related to their appearance or social rank. In Romans 2:11, Paul states that God never acts this way: He judges according to justice, not according to the prestige of the person. 2. It is an injustice that consists of showing undue favor to certain individuals: a master who treats a rich slave better than a poor one (Ephesians 6:9) commits this injustice. God does not tolerate it, even among those who have power. 3. It is also a betrayal of the Christian faith. James 2:1 urges believers to keep their faith in Christ 'free from' this partial treatment. Believing in Jesus while favoring the rich over the poor is a contradiction: it denies the very heart of the Gospel.
G4382.origine: The Greek word is formed from two roots: 'prosopon' (the face, the outward appearance) and 'lambanō' (to receive, to welcome). The initial image is therefore that of 'receiving someone because of their face,' that is, judging based on appearance rather than on inner reality. It is a translation of the Hebrew concept that also emphasizes 'lifting the face' of someone, showing them unjust favor.
G4382.emploi: This word appears four times in the New Testament, always in apostolic epistles (Romans, Ephesians, Colossians, James). It denotes an attitude incompatible with the Christian faith and the justice of God. In Romans 2:11 and Colossians 3:25, Paul establishes that God Himself shows no favoritism: He will judge each one according to their works, without favoring the powerful. In Ephesians 6:9, he reminds masters (who have power over slaves) that God also judges their conduct toward their servants with the same impartiality. In James 2:1, this criticism becomes a moral exhortation: not showing favoritism is to live the Christian faith authentically.
G4382.portee: This word frees the Christian: it affirms that God does not judge them based on their appearance, wealth, or social influence, but on their heart and actions. It also calls them to reject this injustice in their relationships: not to favor the rich or the powerful, not to despise the poor or the weak. It is a call to justice and equality that faith in Jesus should produce within the Christian community.

sens: The front part of the head, the face
The appearance or aspect of a person or thing
The physical presence of someone
The outward appearance or material condition
The surface or visible side of something
G4383.detail: 1. The face is strictly the front part of the head: it is the area where the eyes, mouth, and distinctive features are located. Mark reports that the soldiers covered Jesus' face during His passion (Mark 14:65), and Matthew speaks of the disfigured faces of hypocrites who fast publicly (Matthew 6:16). 2. By extension, the face denotes the general appearance and what it expresses: James compares one who forgets what they have heard to someone who 'looks at their natural face in a mirror' (James 1:23), that is, their own image or appearance. 3. The face can signify personal presence: when Paul says to the Thessalonians 'absent in body but present in spirit,' he adds 'not seeing your face' (1 Thessalonians 2:17), meaning not being in front of you. 4. Figuratively, the face represents the external condition or superficial appearance: 'looking at the face' means judging based on appearance (Matthew 22:16), while Paul speaks of those who 'glory in appearance and not in heart' (2 Corinthians 5:12). 5. The face can designate the surface: 'all who dwell on the face of the whole earth' (Luke 21:35) means on the surface of the earth, everywhere humans live.
G4383.origine: The Greek word πρόσωπον comes from προς (toward, in front of) and ὤψ (the look, the eye), literally 'that which is in front of the look.' It often translates the Hebrew פָּנִים (panim, meaning 'faces' or 'presences'), which in the Hebrew Bible carries an almost personal dimension: to have weight or importance 'face-to-face.' This Hebrew root enriches the Greek word with a significance that goes beyond mere physical traits.
G4383.emploi: The word face appears 72 times in the New Testament, especially in Luke and Paul. It is used first literally for the face: Jesus in Agony 'fell on His face to the ground' (Matthew 26:39), and Peter sees Jesus 'whose face shone like the sun' (Matthew 17:2). Very frequently, it expresses personal presence: 'not seeing someone's face' means not meeting them in person (Acts 20:25, 1 Thessalonians 3:10). Paul enriches this last meaning with Hebraic formulas: 'face to face' or 'before the face' of God (2 Corinthians 10:1, Hebrews 9:24). The word also takes on a moral or metaphorical sense: 'looking at the face' (judging based on appearance), 'receiving a face' (showing partiality), in Galatians 2:6 and Luke 20:21. Finally, it designates the outward appearance of things: 'the face of the earth' (Luke 21:35).
G4383.portee: For the reader, this word opens two important doors. On one hand, the face evokes authentic encounter and relationship: seeing someone in person establishes a communion that words alone cannot replace. This is why Paul longs to see the Thessalonians in person (1 Thessalonians 3:10). On the other hand, the face reminds us of the danger of superficial judgment: it is easy to be impressed by appearance at the expense of true heart. Jesus and Paul rise against this temptation (Matthew 22:16, Galatians 2:6).

sens: To place before oneself, to present publicly
To propose something, to form a design or a plan
G4388.detail:
1. The primary meaning is material: to place something before someone, to put it forward so that it can be seen. It conveys the idea of presenting openly. In Romans 3:25, Christ is "presented" by God as the means of atonement: it is as if God exposes Him to the eyes of all to accomplish His plan of salvation.
2. The reflexive meaning (when the subject acts upon itself) becomes psychological and voluntary: to set a goal, to decide on an intention. In Romans 1:13, Paul says, "I have often formed the plan to go see you": he has placed this intention before his own mind, he has deliberately set it as an objective. It is an act of personal will. In Ephesians 1:9, God has "formed" a design within Himself: He has proposed a plan to Himself that He executes progressively.
G4388.origine: The word combines the prefix "pro-" (before, in front) and the root "tithēmi" (to place, to set). Basic image: to put before oneself. This root is common in Greek and appears in many biblical words. In Hebrew, it often corresponds to "arak" (Exodus 40:4, to arrange) or "sum" (Psalms 54:3, to set). The verb expresses the action of someone who reflects and sets an intention by "placing" it mentally before themselves.
G4388.emploi: The word appears three times in the New Testament. In Romans 1:13, it describes Paul's personal plan: an intention he nurtures and wants to realize. In Romans 3:25, it is used in the passive voice to express that God "presents" Christ as propitiation: there is a public and official nuance here, Christ being put forward for all believers. In Ephesians 1:9, it designates God's eternal purpose in Christ, His benevolent will that He has proposed and that He realizes. The usage thus sweeps both the ordinary personal intention (Paul) and the supreme divine intention (God the Father).
G4388.portee: This word reminds us that forming a plan, having an intention, is a conscious and voluntary action: one must "set" it before oneself. For the Christian, it also shows that God acts with intention and purpose — it is not chance that reigns, but the benevolent will of God, which He "formed" before the foundation of the world. This gives the believer confidence: they live according to a plan, that of God in Christ.

sens: To push someone toward an action, to incite them with kindness
To exhort, to persuade someone to do something
To support someone's courage and determination
G4389.detail:
1. The word evokes the idea of pushing someone forward, giving them direction. It is to incite someone to act, but with a positive and benevolent intention. In Acts 18:27, the brothers "encourage" Apollos to go to Achaia: they push him to continue his teaching ministry.
2. To encourage can also mean to convince someone, to persuade them to make a choice. It is more than just giving advice: it is helping them decide by lifting their hesitations or fears.
3. To support someone's morale and confidence: to give a person the strength or certainty to move forward. This encouragement strengthens determination and gives heart to the work.
G4389.origine: The Greek word is formed from two parts: "pro" (forward) and "trepō" (to turn, to direct). The starting image is that of turning someone forward, giving them direction. It is a word of exhortation, of benevolent counsel that helps to move forward. The "mid." (middle) form used in Acts 18:27 shows that the subject participates in this action: the brothers personally involve themselves by encouraging Apollos.
G4389.emploi: The word appears only once in Acts 18:27 in the New Testament. It is at this precise moment that Apollos, an educated and eloquent Jew from Alexandria, wishes to go to Achaia after receiving the teaching of Aquila and Priscilla in Ephesus. The brothers of the Ephesus community "encourage" him: they support him morally and practically by pushing him to go preach elsewhere. The context shows that this encouragement is not just a simple word, as it is accompanied by a letter of recommendation to facilitate his reception. Biblical encouragement is thus a concrete act, combining verbal exhortation and practical support.
G4389.portee: This word reminds us of the importance of mutual encouragement in the body of Christ. The brothers who encourage Apollos recognize his gifts and release him for greater service. It is a lesson for every Christian: to recognize talent in others and to push them to engage more in the service of the Lord. The encouragement that the brothers offer to Apollos shows that the Christian faith is not individualistic: it is built in community, through mutual support and brotherly exhortation.

sens: To move quickly forward, outpacing others
To arrive first at a destination by running faster
G4390.detail:
1. The word describes the action of running ahead, of rushing forward. It is an active and dynamic run. In Luke 19:4, Zacchaeus "runs ahead" to surpass the crowd and arrive in front of the sycamore before Jesus.
2. The meaning is enriched when several people run together: the one who "runs ahead" surpasses the others and arrives first. In John 20:4, the beloved disciple runs faster than Peter and arrives first at the tomb of Jesus.
G4390.origine: The word comes from two Greek elements: "pro" (forward, in front) and "trechō" (to run). The image is that of someone running forward, who leads the way. The root "trechō" is found in many Greek words related to running and rapid movement. It is a simple and vivid verb, unambiguous: it depicts physical action as it is.
G4390.emploi: The verb appears only twice in the New Testament. In both cases, it describes a precise and visible action: in Luke 19:4, Zacchaeus runs ahead of the crowd to see Jesus; in John 20:4, the beloved disciple runs faster than Peter toward the empty tomb. Both usages show a rapid and eager action, often motivated by an urgent desire or a pressing situation.
G4390.portee: This simple yet vivid verb invites the reader to see the urgency and eagerness of the characters: Zacchaeus burns with the desire to see Jesus, the beloved disciple rushes to the tomb. It reminds us that faith can inspire a joyful haste and a promptness to act, a response without calculation to the call or the event.

sens: That existed or occurred before a given moment or event
State or condition prior to the one being reported
G4391.detail:
1. The word designates what has taken place or existed before a clear temporal reference point. In Luke 23:12, it recalls that Pilate and Herod were enemies previously, that is, before the day of Jesus' judgment. It is a simple indication of past time.
2. More broadly, the word serves to establish a contrast between a previous state and the present situation. In Acts 8:9, Simon practiced magic previously in the city of Samaria, which sets the scene and shows who he was before the arrival of the apostles. The word situates in time what one wishes to evoke.
G4391.origine: The Greek word is formed from three elements: pro (before), hypo (under), and archō (to lead, to be first). The starting image is that of "standing before", of "being in the lead". This compound verb appears only twice in the New Testament, highlighting its rare and literary character.
G4391.emploi: The verb is used only twice in the New Testament. In Luke 23:12, it indicates the past enmity of Pilate and Herod. In Acts 8:9, it describes the activity of Simon the magician before the coming of Philip and the Gospel in Samaria. Both usages clearly situate a reference point in time, always to illuminate the situation at the moment of the narrative.
G4391.portee: This word reminds us that God reads all of history — the past as well as the present. When Luke emphasizes that Pilate and Herod were previously enemies, he shows us a reconciliation that occurs at the moment of Jesus' judgment. When he notes that Simon practiced magic previously, he invites us to see how the Gospel transforms hearts and situations.

sens: pretext, false motive invoked to hide the true intention
action or word displayed to deceive or give a false impression
absence of any plausible excuse or justification
G4392.detail:
1. The word primarily refers to a pretext — a reason given in front to mask one's true motives. The Pharisees make long prayers, but it's only for appearance's sake, so that people admire them (Matthew 23:14): in reality, they are robbing widows. Deceptive appearance is therefore a lie by actions, not just by words.

2. The word also describes the impression one seeks to give, the spectacle one plays. Paul says that some proclaim Christ "for appearance's sake, or sincerely" (Philippians 1:18): they want to appear pious or zealous, not out of true love, but for show.

3. In contrast, the word can also denote the absence of any valid excuse. When Jesus tells the Jews, "they have no excuse for their sin" (John 15:22), He means that there is nothing left to hide behind: the truth has been proclaimed, and only naked guilt remains.
G4392.origine: The word comes from pro- ("in front") and phasis ("what is said, what is shown"). It literally means "what is put forward" to mask what is behind — a facade. In the Hebrew of the Old Testament, parallel words (alila, illa) also mean "pretext" or "alleged motive."
G4392.emploi: The word appears 7 times in the New Testament, mainly in the words of Jesus against Pharisaical hypocrisy (Matthew, Mark, Luke). Three times it refers to the long prayers displayed by the scribes — a religious "appearance" hiding greed (Matthew 23:14, Mark 12:40, Luke 20:47). In John 15:22, it signifies the excuse or justification one might invoke. Paul uses it to describe the imperfect motives of certain preachers (Philippians 1:18) and asserts that he himself never acted out of greed, nor by the false appearance of a noble motive (1 Thessalonians 2:5).
G4392.portee: This word confronts us with the constant danger of hypocrisy — pretending, displaying a virtue one does not have. The Bible invites the believer to reject all "deceptive appearance," not to pray to be seen by men, to serve with a sincere heart, hidden before God alone. It is a call to authenticity: a true Christian life, even hidden, is better than a beautiful facade.

sens: To bring out, extract something from a place
To produce, to spring forth from oneself
In a moral sense: to let escape from one's heart, from one's thoughts
G4393.detail:
1. The verb describes the action of bringing out, extracting something from a place or source. The good man "draws good things from the good treasure of his heart" (Luke 6:45): it is like drawing water from a well, bringing to the surface what was hidden inside.

2. The word evokes the production, the emission of what naturally springs forth from an abundant source. When the heart is full of goodness, good comes out; when it overflows with malice, it is evil that springs forth, without apparent effort.

3. On a moral and spiritual level, the verb shows that our words and actions are not spontaneous inventions, but the result of what fills our inner self. It is the abundance of the heart that "pours out" into words (Luke 6:45): they reveal our true nature.
G4393.origine: The Greek word is formed from the preposition pro ("before", "in front") and the verb pherō ("to carry", "to bring"). The image is that of something being carried or brought "forward", that is brought out. In biblical Hebrew, the verb mâsâ (mâtsa) often translates as "to find" or "to bring out", and it expresses the idea of a discovery or extraction.
G4393.emploi: The verb appears only once in the New Testament according to this record (Luke 6:45). Jesus uses it to teach that our words and actions reveal the true state of our heart: they do not fall from the sky, they come out of it. It is a profound spiritual law: one can only produce what one contains. The Greek Old Testament uses this verb for concrete realities (Proverbs 10:13: the rod draws blows from the one who lacks sense), but the New Testament retains it for the moral and spiritual domain.
G4393.portee: This word reminds us of a disconcerting truth for the Christian: we cannot pretend to be good on the outside if our heart is bad. Our sincere words, our thoughtful actions, reveal what we truly are inside. It is an invitation to let Christ transform our heart, for it is from there that life springs forth (Proverbs 4:23). Before correcting our words, we must correct our source.

sens: the gift of communicating God's will and purpose
the exercise of this gift: speaking in God's name
a message delivered by a prophet
the fulfillment or confirmation of a prophetic word
G4394.detail:
1. Prophecy is primarily a spiritual gift, a capacity that God gives to some to interpret His will and reveal His purpose to men (1 Timothy 4:14: the gift received "by prophecy"). It is an equipping of the Holy Spirit, paralleled with other gifts like faith or tongues (1 Corinthians 13:2).
2. Prophecy then refers to the act of prophesying, that is, speaking God's word in an assembly (1 Corinthians 14:6, 22: prophecy strengthens believers, while tongues primarily signify unbelief). It is a living expression of divine will addressed to the people.
3. Prophecy can also refer to the content, the prophetic message itself: a word, a prediction, a revelation (Revelation 1:3: "the words of the prophecy"). This includes the promises and warnings that a prophet proclaims.
4. By extension, prophecy applies to the fulfillment of an ancient prophetic word (Matthew 13:14: the "prophecy of Isaiah" that is fulfilled), showing that God keeps His promises through the ages.
G4394.origine: The word prophéteia comes from the verb prophêteuô (to prophesy). The root pro means "before, in front" and phêmê or phêmi means "to speak": a prophet speaks in front, he announces in advance or speaks in the name of the one who sends him. In Hebrew and Aramaic, prophecy is called nébouah (נְבוּאָה) or hazôn (חָזוֹן, vision): the prophet receives a revelation from God and transmits it to the people. Biblical prophecy is never a mere human divination, but a word that comes from God.
G4394.emploi: The word prophéteia appears 19 times in the New Testament, mainly in Paul's epistles and in Revelation. In Matthew 13:14, it refers to an Old Testament prophecy that is fulfilled in Jesus. Paul extensively discusses prophecy as a spiritual gift in the assembly (Romans 12:6, 1 Corinthians 12:10, 13:2, 14:6, 14:22): it builds up, exhorts, and consoles believers, unlike tongues. In 1 Thessalonians 5:20 and 1 Timothy 1:18, prophecy guides the life and mission of the disciples. Revelation emphasizes the value of the prophetic words of this book (1:3, 22:7-10, 22:18-19): receiving them with respect is a blessing. The context shows that prophecy is a living and active gift in the apostolic church, not just a phenomenon of the Old Testament.
G4394.portee: Prophecy reminds us that God always speaks to His people, that He guides the Christian assembly through men and women whom He inspires. It calls the believer to listen to God's voice and to respect His messengers. Finally, by showing how ancient prophecies are fulfilled, it affirms God's faithfulness: His words never fall to the ground and are realized according to His plan.

sens: To announce the words of God, to convey His message
To predict the future in the name of God
To speak under the inspiration of the Holy Spirit in a gathering
G4395.detail:
1. To prophesy is primarily to speak in the name of God, to convey His will and thoughts: it is to 'declare forth', to publicly express what God reveals. In Matthew 7:22, people claim to have prophesied in the name of Jesus, meaning they spoke with His authority. Mark 7:6 reminds us that Isaiah prophesied about the hypocrites, meaning he announced what God judged about them.
2. To prophesy can also mean to announce in advance what will happen: to predict the future. John 11:51 shows Caiaphas who 'prophesies that Jesus should die for the nation', without even understanding it himself — it is God who speaks through him.
3. In the Church, prophesying becomes exercising a spiritual gift: to speak publicly, to edify others through inspired words. In 1 Corinthians 14:24, if all prophesy and an unbeliever comes in, 'he is convinced, judged by all' — the prophetic word confronts and convinces. The four daughters of Philip (Acts 21:9) 'prophesied' as an expression of their connection to the Spirit.
G4395.origine: The word comes from 'prophet' (prophêtês), one who speaks for another, especially for God. In Hebrew, the Old Testament uses the verb naba to describe the action of the prophet: to convey the divine word. The family of the word includes 'prophecy' (the prophetic word itself) and 'prophet' (one who prophesies). The Greek verb prophêteuô captures this idea exactly: to speak as a spokesperson for God.
G4395.emploi: The verb appears 27 times in the New Testament, mainly in the Gospels and 1 Corinthians. Matthew and Mark often show it in the context of false prophets or Jesus applying the words of true prophets to the Pharisees (Matthew 7:22, Mark 7:6). Acts and 1 Corinthians describe the gift of prophecy as a manifestation of the Holy Spirit in the Christian assembly (Acts 19:6, 21:9): it is a charisma to cultivate and regulate for edification (1 Corinthians 14:1-5, 14:24-31). In Revelation 10:11 and 11:3, prophets fulfill a future divine mission. Luke 1:67 shows Zechariah prophesying under the Spirit at the time of John the Baptist's birth.
G4395.portee: For the Christian reader, understanding biblical prophecy means grasping that God has always spoken to His people: through prophets in the past, through His Spirit in the Church today. This word reminds us that prophecy is not primarily about predicting the future, but proclaiming the word of God and convincing hearts. It is a gift to desire (1 Corinthians 14:1) for the edification of the assembly, not a power to impress.

sens: One who speaks in the name of God, who conveys His words and will
One who announces the future according to divine revelation
Author of the prophetic books of the Old Testament
Spiritual leader recognized as a bearer of the divine word
Inspired poet, wise one who interprets divine plans
G4396.detail: 1. A prophet is primarily someone whom God has chosen to be His spokesperson: he faithfully conveys what God entrusts to him. Elisha is called 'the prophet' (Luke 4:27) because he spoke in the name of God; John the Baptist is also a prophet (Luke 1:76) because he announces the coming of the Lord. 2. The prophet announces what is to come, by virtue of the knowledge that God gives him: when Jesus says 'there have been prophets and kings who desired to see what you see' (Luke 10:24), He speaks of those who predicted His coming. 3. The term also refers to the authors of the books of the Old Testament known as 'the Prophets': Jesus refers to 'the law of Moses, the prophets, and the psalms' (Luke 24:44) to speak of all that concerns Him. 4. It is a recognized role: the prophet is asked to confirm what is presumed to be the word of God, as when the crowd asks if John is the expected prophet (John 1:21-25). 5. The prophet receives honor and respect: Jesus says that 'a prophet is not without honor, except in his own country' (Mark 6:4), showing that his word should be listened to with reverence.
G4396.origine: The Greek word comes from the verb πρόφημι 'to say beforehand, to speak in the name of', composed of πρό ('before, in place of') and φημί ('to speak'). The original image is that of someone who speaks for another, who anticipates or states what is to be. In Hebrew, the prophet is called נָבִיא (nabi), whose etymology suggests 'one who is called' or 'one who proclaims'. The Septuagint (Greek translation of the Old Testament) systematically uses prophētēs to translate nabi, establishing a strong link between the Hebrew conception of the prophet and the Greek word.
G4396.emploi: The word prophet appears 145 times in the New Testament Segond 1910. It primarily applies to the prophets of the Old Testament — Jeremiah, Isaiah, Moses, Elisha — whose writings and words are cited as the fulfillment of divine will (Matthew 1:22; Luke 4:27). It then designates John the Baptist, a transitional figure between the Old and New Testaments, who prepares the way for the Lord (Luke 1:76). Jesus Himself is identified as the expected prophet: 'This man is truly the prophet,' says the crowd (John 6:14); Moses had foretold His coming (Acts 7:37). In the apostolic Church, the term extends to Christian prophets who receive the gift of prophecy from the Holy Spirit (Acts 15:32; 1 Corinthians 12:28). The term also extends to encompass all prophetic writings: 'the Prophets' are cited alongside the Law and the Psalms as testimony to Jesus (Luke 24:44; Romans 3:21).
G4396.portee: To recognize someone as a prophet is to accept that he speaks in the name of God Himself: it is a matter of total trust and obedience to the received word. For the Christian, understanding that Jesus is the prophet par excellence (much more than that, for He is the Son of God) changes everything: it is to listen not to a word about God, but to the Word of God in person. The very existence of prophets in the Church shows that God continues to speak to His people through the gift of the Holy Spirit.

sens: That which comes from a prophet, given by a prophet
Concerning prophecy, the prophetic message
That which announces the future, revealing what is to come
G4397.detail:
1. Prophetic refers to that which comes from a prophet — a word, a writing, a message that God has entrusted to the one He has sent to speak in His name. In 2 Peter 1:19, Peter calls the entirety of the messages received by the prophets of the Old Testament the "prophetic word": it is not a human invention, but a divine communication.
2. The word refers to the very nature of prophecy: it is revelation, illumination, certainty. When Peter says that we should pay attention to this word "as to a lamp shining in a dark place," he emphasizes that prophecy illuminates the darkness of doubt and ignorance.
3. The prophetic word also carries the idea of promise and fulfillment: it announces what is to happen, God's plans for the future, and invites the reader to trust and be vigilant while awaiting the realization of these promises.
G4397.origine: The word comes from prophētēs ("prophet"), which designates one whom God sends to speak in His name. The root evokes the idea of "speaking beforehand," of saying in advance, or of "speaking in the place of" someone. Prophetic is the adjective that characterizes everything belonging to the prophet and his message: a prophetic word is a word from the prophet, carrying the authority and truth of God.
G4397.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament, in 2 Peter 1:19. Peter uses it to qualify the word of the prophets of the Old Testament — these messages received by men whom God had chosen to reveal His will and plans. By using it here, Peter affirms the absolute authority and reliability of the prophetic Scriptures: they are not human conjectures, but the certain word of God. This word, although given in the past, remains current and relevant for believers of all times, like a lamp shining in the darkness.
G4397.portee: For the Christian reader, this word reminds us that the Scriptures of the Old Testament are not just historical documents among others: they are prophetic words, that is, revelations from God given by those He has chosen. This invites us to read them with respect and attention, as messages addressed to our faith today. It is also an invitation to scrutinize the promises and prophetic fulfillments: they illuminate our path until the day Christ returns.

sens: A woman who receives and transmits the words of God
A woman who exercises the prophetic ministry
A woman who falsely claims to be a prophet (wrongly or abusively)
G4398.detail:
1. The prophetess is a woman to whom God entrusts His words to convey to His people. Anna, at the temple in Jerusalem (Luke 2:36), embodied this calling: she recognized Jesus as the Messiah and praised God for His salvation. She is a woman endowed with the Holy Spirit to speak on God's behalf.
2. The prophetic ministry among women exists in the Old Testament (the prophetess Deborah judged Israel, Judges 4:4) and continues in the New Testament. Prophetesses could teach, exhort, and reveal the secrets of the heart.
3. Jezebel in Revelation 2:20 shows the counterexample: she usurps the title of prophetess to seduce believers and lead them into idolatry and immorality. She is a false prophetess who abuses her influence.
G4398.origine: The word comes from prophḗtēs, "one who speaks in the name of God" (Greek pro-, "before," and phḗmi, "to speak"). The feminine form prophḗtis derives naturally from it. In the Greek of the Old Testament, this word translates the Hebrew nebî'āh, the woman prophet.
G4398.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament. Anna, an elderly and pious woman, is presented as a true prophetess who serves God constantly through prayer and fasting, recognizing the fulfillment of the promises. Jezebel, in contrast, is a false prophetess who taught in the church of Thyatira, preaching immorality and idolatry. These two uses show the authenticity and counterfeit of the female prophetic ministry.
G4398.portee: Anna reminds us that God grants the prophetic gift to faithful and vigilant women of faith, to recognize His work and guide His people. Jezebel warns against false prophets who seduce with deceptive words: believers must discern between true prophecy, marked by piety and truth, and imposture, which leads to sin.

sens: To go ahead of someone by speaking or acting before they do
To go to meet someone to do something before they ask for it
G4399.detail:
1. The word describes the action of speaking or acting before someone else does: one "goes ahead". It is a form of taking initiative. In Matthew 17:25, Jesus "prevents" Simon Peter by asking him a question about the temple tax before Peter says anything — He anticipates Peter's thoughts and speaks first.
2. More broadly, "to prevent" means to meet an intention or request: to do something before one is asked, like a gesture of waiting or service. It is acting in a somewhat "preventive" manner to anticipate the need or question of another.
G4399.origine: The word combines the Greek prefix "pro" (before) and the root "phthánō" (to reach, to go ahead, to arrive first). This root evokes the image of one who runs faster and arrives before others. In the Greek Old Testament, this word often translates the Hebrew verb "qadam," which also means "to go before, to anticipate." The simple word "phthánō" is more common in the New Testament, but its compound form with "pro" reinforces the idea of going ahead.
G4399.emploi: This verb appears only once in the Greek New Testament, in Matthew 17:25. It describes a crucial moment: Jesus and Peter enter a house, and before Peter raises the question of the temple tax, Jesus Himself asks him a question that shows He understands Peter's concern. It is an act of insight and kindness — Jesus "prevents" Peter by speaking first, thus showing him His knowledge of the situation and guiding the disciple's reflection.
G4399.portee: This passage reveals the nature of Jesus: He knows thoughts and concerns even before they are expressed. For the reader, this affirms that Jesus is not just another teacher, but someone who reads hearts. It invites the believer to trust: our concerns are never hidden from Jesus; He anticipates them with His wisdom and grace.

sens: Prepare someone to be whipped by tying or positioning them
Strip the body in view of punishment
G4385.detail:
1. The word evokes the action of stretching, extending, or arranging something — here, a person's body — in anticipation of punishment. In Acts 22:25, Paul is "exposed" to the whip: the Roman soldiers bind or position him to be flogged, a terrible act that precedes the blows of the rods. It is a brutal preparation for corporal punishment.
2. The meaning extends to the idea of putting someone in a vulnerable position, stripped bare, subjected to punishment — a physical and humiliating exposure before torture. The context of Acts emphasizes the injustice: Paul, a Roman citizen protected by law, should never be "exposed" in such a manner without trial.
G4385.origine: The Greek word is composed of "pro-" (before, in front of) and "teinô" (to stretch, to extend). It evokes the image of stretching something forward or arranging it. In ancient Greek, this verb applies to concrete acts: to present, to offer, to extend. Here it takes on a threatening and violent sense, that of preparing a body for torture.
G4385.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 22:25. Paul, arrested in Jerusalem and brought to the Roman fortress, cries out his status as a Roman citizen just as the soldiers bind him to whip him. This unique occurrence underscores the urgency of his appeal to his legal rights: its usage is dramatic and reveals a well-known Roman military practice. The verb describes the phase of preparation for corporal punishment, even before the blows begin.
G4385.portee: This word recalls the sufferings endured by Paul for his faith and exposes the injustice of human authorities. It also shows how Paul cleverly used his Roman citizenship to escape this torture — a lesson on the importance of knowing and invoking one's rights. It is a stark detail that confronts us with the reality of primitive persecution.

sens: What occurred before a given moment
What was in the first position in time or order
What belongs to an earlier, bygone era
G4386.detail:
1. The word refers to an event or action that preceded another: Paul states that he was previously a blasphemer (1 Timothy 1:13), before receiving God's mercy and becoming an apostle. It simply places a fact in the past.
2. It can also designate what comes first in a logical or temporal series: the priests first offered sacrifices for their own sins, then for those of the people (Hebrews 7:27). Here the word marks the order of actions.
3. Used to qualify an entire era that has passed: Christians remember their early days of spiritual enlightenment and persecution (Hebrews 10:32), or the life once lived in ignorance (1 Peter 1:14). It is a bygone past that contrasts with the present.
G4386.origine: The Greek word πρότερον comes from πρό (pro), which means "before," and the comparative ending -τερον (-teron). It literally expresses the idea of what is "further ahead," that is, earlier. It carries the spatial notion of what is in front, advanced, that has occurred first. It is an adverb that marks time and order.
G4386.emploi: This word appears 5 times in the New Testament, mainly in the epistles: 1 Timothy, Hebrews, and 1 Peter. Paul uses it to recall his own past as a persecutor (1 Timothy 1:13), raising a powerful contrast with his transformation. The author of Hebrews uses it to clarify the order of Christ's sacrificial actions and to refer to the early times of the readers' faith. In 1 Peter, it refers to the former life lived without knowledge of God. In all cases, the word establishes a break: a before and an after, the past and the present.
G4386.portee: This word invites believers to measure the journey taken. It emphasizes that the past, even if marked by error, ignorance, or sin, does not define the present destiny. Paul uses it to show that God's grace radically transforms: the one who previously persecuted has become an apostle. For the reader, it is an invitation to see their past as something that has been surpassed, and to view their present as a break from that bygone time.

sens: That which occurred before in time
Before, in an order of events or priorities
Earlier, which preceded a current situation or state
G4387.detail:
1. This word designates what comes before in time, what has already taken place. The Son of Man, in John 6:62, asks: "And if you see the Son of Man ascending where he was previously?" — that is, before, prior to his earthly coming. This is the simplest meaning: formerly, before now.
2. Sometimes it marks the logical or temporal order of a succession: in 2 Corinthians 1:15, Paul says: "I wanted to go to you first," which means as a priority, first rather than later. It expresses the first place in a sequence.
3. It can qualify a state or a past phase: in Ephesians 4:22, it speaks of "your former life," that of before conversion. In 1 Peter 1:14, it refers to the "former lusts," the old desires one had when not knowing Christ.
G4387.origine: The word comes from an ancient Greek root meaning "before." It is the comparative form of the adjective "old": "older" becomes "old" then "before." In Hebrew, it often translates רִאשׁוֹן (ri-chôn), which means "first," or לִפָנִים (li-fanîm), "formerly." It is a word of position and natural succession.
G4387.emploi: This word appears six times in Greek in the New Testament. It is primarily used adverbially, that is, as an adverb modifying the verb: "ascend previously" (John 6:62), "known previously" (John 9:8), "having preached previously" (Galatians 4:13). It can also be an adjective in the expression "your former life" (Ephesians 4:22) or "the former days" (Hebrews 10:32). Its usage covers all temporal contexts: the divine past of Christ, the personal past of believers, the order of actions.
G4387.portee: This word invites the believer to meditate on the path he has traveled and the change that Christ works in him. Recognizing his former life, his old lusts, is the first step of sanctification. Understanding that the Son of Man was "previously" affirms his divine eternity.
